The Italian DPA fined a sole trader EUR 3,000 for video surveillance at its premises. The system had 14 working cameras inside and outside the site, could monitor employees' activity remotely, and could also capture a public road. It was installed without the collective agreement or labour inspectorate authorisation required by Article 4 of the Workers' Statute, which Article 114 of the Italian Privacy Code incorporates. The DPA found breaches of the lawfulness principle (Art. 5(1)(a)) and cited Art. 5(1)(c) in its operative part. The trader had removed the cameras and deleted the footage, and the decision was ordered published on the DPA website.

The Guardia di Finanza inspected a shop in March 2019 and found a video surveillance system with 12 cameras, 4 of them working, with no information signs and no authorisation from the Labour Inspectorate or union agreement. The Garante opened sanction proceedings; the owner submitted no defence and did not cooperate. The Garante declared the processing unlawful for breach of Articles 5 and 13 GDPR and Article 114 of the Code. It imposed a fine of EUR 20,000 and ordered publication of the decision on its website.

A healthcare trust notified a personal data breach: a patient collecting her report was handed an envelope containing a digital medium (CD/DVD) with another patient's neuroradiology exam, due to human error when packing the envelope. The Garante found unlawful disclosure of health data to a third party and breach of the integrity/confidentiality principle and security obligations. It imposed a fine of EUR 7,000, noting the single person affected, absence of intent, remedial measures and high cooperation. No corrective orders were imposed and the decision is published in full.

A former employee of the municipality of Villabate complained that the municipality sent a letter about the garnishment of part of his salary to his new employer, disclosing alleged debts and the reasons he left. He also complained that the municipality had not properly appointed a data protection officer (DPO) or published the DPO's contact details. The Garante found that the disclosures to the bank and the new employer had no valid legal basis, and that the municipality appointed its DPO late, chose a person in a conflict of interests, and failed to communicate and publish the DPO's contact details. It fined the municipality EUR 6,000 and ordered publication of the decision. No further corrective measures were needed because the conduct had ceased.

Local police inspected a shop run by Singh Market S.r.l. on 23 September 2021 and found eight active CCTV cameras with no information signs. The company did not submit any defence and did not cooperate with the Garante, and it did not show that it had complied with the notice obligation. The Garante found breaches of the transparency principle in Art. 5(1)(a) and of the information duty in Art. 13 GDPR. It imposed a fine of EUR 2,000 and ordered publication of the decision on its website.

Datatilsynet issued a serious criticism (reprimand) to 3F Østfyn after a member's new name was printed on the union magazine and the magazine was sent to the member's old address, where a former violent partner still lived. The member had changed name and address and obtained address protection in the CPR register, but by human error only the name was updated in the CRM system. The authority found that the CRM system kept the last known address as default without verification, and that 3F lacked procedures and technical safeguards for such updates, breaching the accuracy principle and the security requirement. No fine was imposed.

In a procedure under Article 60 GDPR, the Swedish DPA reprimanded Klarna Bank AB for not providing information on the recipients to which personal data had been disclosed when replying to an access request under Article 15 GDPR.

The Finnish DPA fined a magazine publisher €85,000 for deficiencies in facilitating the exercise of data subject rights. The controller, among other things, required data subjects to print, fill, sign and send a paper form to have their data deleted.

An applicant who took a practical exam asked the college for copies of the video recordings of the exam. The college refused, saying the recordings also showed other students and could not be edited to show only the applicant, although it had given the applicant written feedback on the exam. The Deputy Data Protection Ombudsman held that the college had not shown concrete grounds under Article 15(4) for refusing access and ordered it to give the applicant the recordings insofar as the applicant appears in them.
The Belgian Data Protection Authority ordered a company to comply with Article 13(1)(b) GDPR and to publish the contact details of their DPO on their website.

Following a complaint, the Romanian authority investigated a financial institution that had installed audio-video cameras in employees' offices. It found the controller had not shown that the stated purpose was justified, that less intrusive means had failed first, or that it met the principles of Article 5 and the lawfulness conditions of Article 6 GDPR and Article 5 of Law 190/2018. The controller was fined RON 19,772.4 (about EUR 4,000).

In October 2020 the Belgian railway company SNCB emailed holders of the free Hello Belgium Railpass a message mixing Covid-19 health advice with promotion of travel destinations, with no easy way to opt out. The Inspection Service found no valid legal basis and no facilitated right to object. The Litigation Chamber rejected the SNCB's reliance on contract performance and its argument that the email was not direct marketing. It found breaches of Articles 5, 6, 12 and 21 GDPR and fined SNCB EUR 10,000, noting the very wide reach (3.6 million Railpasses). The Market Court later reduced the fine.

A person who requested copies of criminal case documents from the Supreme Court was asked for a personal identity number and home address for invoicing, and complained about this and about how recipients of documents are recorded. The Deputy Data Protection Ombudsman found it has no competence over the court's disclosure of case documents, which is a judicial task under Article 55(3) GDPR, and closed that part of the matter. It found that collecting the identity number for fees charged after the request had a legal basis under section 29 of the Data Protection Act and was lawful under Article 6(1)(c) GDPR. It asked the Supreme Court to reassess the risk of retaliation against document requesters and report by 15 September 2022.

The Romanian authority concluded an investigation in March 2022 into Megareduceri TV S.R.L. after several complainants received unsolicited commercial SMS messages on their personal phone numbers promoting a website, without having consented. The company confirmed receipt of the authority's requests but did not answer them, so it was fined for failing to provide the requested information. The fine was 19,795.6 lei (about EUR 4,000). The authority also ordered corrective measures to ensure processing complies with the GDPR and that phone numbers are not used for direct marketing without prior express consent.

This is the follow-up decision on the fine in the Seesaw student system case. An earlier decision of 16 December 2021 had found that the City of Reykjavík's processing of schoolchildren's personal data in Seesaw breached data protection law, and had ordered the accounts closed and the data deleted. In this decision Persónuvernd decided whether to impose an administrative fine and how much. It considered the City's objections point by point under the Article 83(2) factors. It imposed a fine of ISK 5,000,000, payable within a month. The decision stresses that children's data was involved, that sensitive data was likely to be entered, and that data was transferred to the US without adequate safeguards.

A doctor complained that HEI – Medical Travel had obtained, stored and used his email address for a marketing email, and had not handled his access request. HEI's employee had copied doctors' email addresses from the closed area of the Icelandic Medical Association's website using a relative's doctor login. Persónuvernd found there was no legal basis for the processing and that the access request breached Article 15 GDPR, since the data was deleted after the request and no access was given. It imposed an administrative fine of ISK 1,500,000.

The Belgian DPA held, among others, that a controller is not obliged to report a data breach which results from listing the recipients of an email in CC instead of BCC if the email is only received by a small group (16 people).
The Finnish DPA fined a telemarketing company €8,300 for not giving the data subject access to the sales call recording even after the DPA ordered it to do so.

An employee of a provincial fire service administration complained that her superior inspected the browsing history on her work computer without informing her, and that her access request for copies of disciplinary decisions was not answered. The Authority found the Fire Service Headquarters, as controller, in breach of the principles of lawfulness, transparency and security, of the rules on the data protection officer's involvement, and of the right of access. It ordered compliance measures and a reply to the access request, and imposed three fines totalling EUR 35,000.

A complainant who took out a mobile and fibre portability contract at a point of sale (a Vodafone authorised distributor) later found four further Vodafone contracts in his name, dated 17 and 29 October, 4 November and 22 December 2020, which he had not signed or agreed to, and which were charged to him. The AEPD held that the company had processed his data without a legal basis, rejecting its argument that it was only a processor acting for Vodafone because it decided itself how and why the data were processed. It imposed a fine of EUR 15,000 for infringement of Article 6(1) GDPR, citing negligence as an aggravating factor.

A private childcare nursery operator, Educationest s.r.l., emailed the families of the children in an educator's group that she was pregnant and had to leave her role immediately as high-risk work. The educator, who had not been consulted and had not yet told her own family, complained to the Garante. The Garante found that disclosing her pregnancy to third parties lacked a valid legal basis and breached the lawfulness and data minimisation principles. It imposed a fine of EUR 1,000 and ordered publication of the decision on its website.

An employee of the Ministry of Defence complained about two disclosures of his data. In the first, health-related information (a court ruling reference, a request for medical checks and a medical visit summons) was passed to the president and a member of a competitive-exam board. In the second, an email with criminal-proceedings data was mistakenly forwarded to a serviceman who had no right to it. The Garante found that both disclosures lacked a legal basis and breached Articles 5(1)(a), 6, 9 and 10 GDPR and Articles 2-ter, 2-sexies and 2-octies of the Code. It fined the Ministry EUR 10,000, ordered publication of the decision, and imposed no corrective measures given the Ministry's assurances and new procedures.

INAIL, the Italian workplace-injury insurer, notified the Garante of three personal data breaches in 2019-2020 in its online 'Sportello Virtuale Lavoratori' service, through which users could see other users' injury and occupational-disease files, including health information. The Garante found breaches of the lawfulness and integrity/confidentiality principles, of the security obligations and of the rules on the legal basis for health data. It fined INAIL and ordered publication of the decision. The Rome Tribunal reduced the fine to EUR 20,000; the Court of Cassation (judgment 24998 of 4 September 2026) confirmed that reduction and sent another point back to the Tribunal. The Garante's published text now shows the reduced amount.

A complainant teacher was affected when a school timetable file containing a reference to her Law 104 disability-benefit status, and similar information about other teachers, was published by mistake in the teachers-only area of the school's electronic register. The school said it was a material error, since an internal version was published instead of the version with sensitive data removed. The Garante found that the school had unlawfully processed personal and health data, in breach of Articles 5, 6 and 9 GDPR and Articles 2-ter and 2-sexies of the Codice. It imposed a fine of EUR 2,500, taking into account the sensitivity of the data, the mitigating facts, and ordered publication of the decision on its website.

A former employee of the Comune di Partanna complained that a municipal council resolution published on the council's website named him in full, when only his initials should have appeared. The resolution also described details of an employment dispute and a disciplinary procedure. The Garante found the online publication unlawful: it lacked a valid legal basis and was not limited to what was necessary, breaching the GDPR principles and Article 6, plus the Italian Code's Article 2-ter. It imposed a fine of EUR 2,000 and ordered publication of the decision on the Garante's website. The municipality had already corrected the document after being notified.

Police inspecting a food and drink premises on 19 February 2021 found two working CCTV cameras and no information signs about video surveillance. The Garante found that the company had breached the transparency principle and the duty to inform data subjects about the cameras. The company later said it had installed the signs and, in March 2022, that the business had permanently closed. The Garante imposed a fine of EUR 2,000 and ordered publication of the decision on its website.

A publisher's digital legal-news service posted in full a Court of Cassation order on the same-sex adoption of a minor, with the identifying details of the family, despite the court's annotation requiring anonymisation. The family complained to the Garante, also about an incomplete answer to their access requests. The Garante found the processing unlawful, banned further processing, issued a warning for the incomplete and late reply to the data subject rights request, and imposed a fine of EUR 40,000. The publisher had removed the order the day after the request and cooperated.

Nos, a telemarketing agency working for Vodafone, bought about 3.8 million contact records from two UK list providers and passed them on to Vodafone as an autonomous controller. It gave the individuals no information notice and obtained no consent for the disclosure. The Garante rejected Nos's argument that it acted only as Vodafone's processor. It found violations of Articles 13, 14, 5(1)(a), 6 and 7 GDPR, banned further processing of the acquired data and fined Nos EUR 20,000. The fine was kept low because the company was inactive and going into liquidation.

The hospital notified two data breaches in which newsletters to patients of its neurology unit and its transplant and bariatric surgery unit were sent with recipients' email addresses in the visible CC field instead of BCC. This revealed to recipients that others were patients of those units, i.e. health information. The Garante rejected the hospital's arguments, found a breach of Art. 5(1)(f) and Art. 9 GDPR, and fined it EUR 70,000. No corrective orders were issued since the conduct had ended and remedial measures were taken. The decision is to be published in full.

After a complaint from a candidate in a public selection procedure, the Garante found that the Comune had published online lists of admitted and non-admitted candidates, which were also indexed by search engines, with no legal basis. The Comune also gave an inadequate reply to the candidate's erasure request. The Garante imposed a fine of EUR 3,000 for breaches of Articles 5(1)(a), 6(1)(e) and 17 GDPR and of the former Article 2-ter of the Italian Privacy Code. No corrective measures were ordered because the lists had been removed, but the decision was ordered to be published on the Garante's website.

A complaint said the school's special-needs working group (GLO) meeting calendars, sent by email to parents, teachers and specialists, listed in clear the names of all pupils with disabilities by class, and some of them showed the parents' email addresses. The Garante found that the school sent these calendars to parents of other pupils and to people not entitled to know the pupils' health situation, which was an unlawful disclosure of health data and email addresses. The school was ordered to pay a fine of EUR 1,500, and the decision is to be published on the Garante's website.

Amiu S.p.A., the in-house waste collection company of the Municipality of Taranto, installed video surveillance cameras to catch illegal waste dumping and published videos and images on its Facebook profile in which people were identifiable. The Garante found no legal basis for the publication and a breach of purpose limitation. It also found that the company's role was never defined under Article 28 for about ten years, that it appointed a video system supplier as processor without authorisation from the controller, and that it had not designated a data protection officer. It fined the company EUR 20,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

After a report, the Garante found that the municipality of Taranto, through its waste-collection company Amiu, ran a video surveillance system (including smart camera traps) against illegal waste dumping without giving data subjects proper information, without a data processing agreement with the company until January 2022, and without a data protection impact assessment. It found breaches of Articles 5, 12, 13, 14, 28 and 35 GDPR and fined the municipality EUR 20,000. It ordered the municipality within 30 days to ensure proper information notices (including signage) and to carry out a DPIA, and ordered publication of the decision. The Facebook publication by the company is dealt with in a separate decision.

The Spanish DPA held that sending someone notifications regarding monetary fines directed at another person constitutes a violation of Article 5(1)(f) GDPR. As the respective data was not rectified in time after receiving a complaint, it also resulted in a breach of Article 32 GDPR.

The Danish DPA learned in August 2021 that a youth crisis centre, Joannahuset, had asked for a young person's name and national ID number (CPR) by SMS to verify identity before providing shelter. The DPA opened an own-initiative case, saying SMS transmission of confidential data carries a significant risk and that Article 32 normally requires a secure transmission solution. However, it accepted that in this acute, one-off situation with no safer option available in time, the young person's interests outweighed data protection, so it found no grounds for criticism.

The Spanish DPA fined the owner of a commercial website €1,800 for processing personal data and using of cookies without a legal basis and for not providing sufficient information to the data subject per Article 13 GDPR.

Datatilsynet carried out a written supervision of Gladsaxe Kommune's management of access rights for school-area systems, focusing on the ESDH system SBSYS. It found that the municipality had not removed a former employee's access rights to SBSYS after the employee left, and had not carried out adequate follow-up or review of rights of former staff. Datatilsynet found this breached the security requirement in Article 32(1) GDPR and issued a reprimand (kritik). No fine was imposed.

A German shareholder of Mowi ASA complained that the company had not answered his access request and had not told him the purposes of the processing of his data, which Mowi had obtained through his bank via its share register provider. Mowi admitted it had not provided the Article 14 information and argued that exceptions in Article 14(5)(a) and (c) applied, which Datatilsynet rejected. Datatilsynet issued a reprimand for infringing Article 14 GDPR and ordered Mowi to take measures so that shareholders receive all information required by Article 14, reporting back within four weeks. No fine was imposed.
The claimant exercised his rights of access and deletion. The right of access was granted. However, the right for deletion could not be granted in accordance with Article 17 GDPR.

The Danish Financial Supervisory Authority (Finanstilsynet) disclosed to a journalist, in response to a freedom-of-information request, whistleblower-related email addresses. Redactions had been applied by blacking out text in PDFs, but the underlying data could be read by hovering over the redacted areas. Datatilsynet found that the authority had not taken appropriate technical and organisational measures under Article 32(1) GDPR, because it lacked clear anonymisation instructions and did not know hidden data could be recovered. It issued a serious criticism (reprimand) and no fine.

The Data Protection Authority decided that cases concerning camera surveillance by neighbours are to be dealt with by the police, due to the Act of March 2007 (regulating the installation of surveillance cameras).

The Romanian supervisory authority finished an investigation into IKEA România in March 2022 after a complaint from a person who had repeatedly asked for a user account to be deleted. The controller could not show that it replied within the legal time limit to the erasure requests, which breaches Article 12(3) GDPR. It was fined RON 4,949 (about EUR 1,000) and ordered to take the measures needed to respect data subjects' rights in all cases.

The Spanish DPA issued a fine of €1800 against an online clothes store for processing personal data without data subjects' consent, for failing to have a privacy policy, and for the use of non-essential cookies without providing appropriate information through a cookie banner.

Following a press revelation concerning the public leak of sensitive health and administrative data belonging to nearly 500,000 patients, the CNIL carried out investigations into a medical software provider acting as a data processor for medical laboratories. The CNIL found breaches of Article 28(3) GDPR for lack of compliant data processing agreements, Article 29 GDPR for extracting patient data beyond controller instructions during migrations, and Article 32 GDPR due to severe technical and organizational security failures on an FTP server. The CNIL imposed an administrative fine of EUR 1,500,000 and ordered the publication of the decision for two years before anonymization.

The Spanish DPA fined an adult content website €8000 for its unlawful use of cookies and providing insufficient information related to their nature and purposes, as well for having an outdated privacy policy, which was based on data protection laws prior to the entry into force of the GDPR.

The Austrian DPA held that the operator of a search engine must delete a link to a database which contains the home address of the data subject if the latter fears for his physical integrity after receiving a death threat.

The Romanian supervisory authority finished an investigation in March 2022 into a property owners' association in Cluj-Napoca. The investigation followed a complaint that the association had published images of the complainant from its video surveillance system on the building's Facebook group. The association confirmed receiving the authority's requests but never answered them, so it did not provide the requested information. It was fined 2,474.5 lei (about EUR 500) and ordered to send all the requested information within 5 working days.

The Dutch DPA investigated the Fraude Signalering Voorziening (FSV), a fraud-signalling application used by the Tax and Customs Administration until February 2020. It found that the Minister of Finance, as controller, processed personal data in FSV from 4 November 2013 to 27 February 2020 without a legal basis, without a specified purpose, with inaccurate data and with excessive retention. It also found inadequate security (access, logging and log checks) and that the data protection officer was not involved properly or in time in the DPIA. The AP imposed six separate administrative fines totalling EUR 3,700,000, raising the base amounts for the nature, gravity and duration of the breaches, negligence, the data categories and, for some, earlier relevant infringements.

During an inspection campaign on whistleblowing software, the Garante checked a hospital in Perugia and its provider ISWEB. It found the hospital processed personal data via the whistleblowing application without a specific privacy notice, without recording it in the register of processing, without a DPIA, and without adequate security (navigation logs kept on firewalls, credentials of a departed RPCT still active). It found breaches of Articles 5(1)(a) and (f), 13, 14, 25, 30, 32 and 35 GDPR and fined the hospital EUR 40,000. No corrective measures were ordered because the conduct had ended and the hospital had cooperated.

During an inspection campaign on whistleblowing software, the Garante examined ISWEB S.p.A., which supplies a whistleblowing platform to clients including the Perugia hospital and acts as their processor. ISWEB used a hosting provider (Seeweb) without a proper Article 28 arrangement, both for its own processing as controller and for processing done for clients as processor, including without the hospital's prior authorisation. ISWEB argued the breaches were merely formal and that the IP addresses involved were not personal data, but the Garante rejected this. It found the Article 28 infringements, fined ISWEB EUR 40,000, ordered it to bring the processing into compliance within 30 days and report back, and ordered publication of the decision.

A commercial agent complained that the company cut off her work email account without notice, kept it alive, and ignored her requests for access to her data. The company also failed to answer the Garante's information requests, so the Garante used the Guardia di Finanza to serve them. The Garante found breaches of fairness and storage limitation, of the duty to inform, of the access right and response deadlines, and of the duty to answer the authority. It declared the processing unlawful, ordered access for the complainant, deactivation of the account with automatic notices, a ban on further processing of the extracted data and better procedures, and fined the company EUR 50,000.

A individual complained that Made in Italy s.r.l.s. called him twice for promotion without consent and ignored his access, erasure and objection requests. The company also never answered the Garante's request for information and did not defend itself. The Garante found breaches of Articles 15, 17, 21, 6 and 7 GDPR and of the Code (Art. 130(3), 157). It issued a warning, ordered the company to answer the complainant, banned further processing of his data, and fined it EUR 20,000, with publication of the decision.

A debtor complained that the bank Findomestic contacted his wife, who was guarantor on only one of his loans, about another loan for which he alone was liable. The bank explained that a staff member mistakenly entered the wife's phone number as a contact, so two SMS messages about payment status were sent to her in October 2020. The Garante found the processing unlawful and in breach of the principles of lawfulness, fairness, transparency and data minimisation. It fined the bank EUR 10,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

A man who had bought goods from the company asked it on 10 July 2020 for access to his personal data and related information under Article 15 GDPR, and the company did not answer within the legal time limit. During the procedure the company only listed categories of data, called the request unfounded and pretextual, and argued the data were already known to him and belonged to his firm. The Garante rejected these arguments, since the request concerned his own personal data, and found breaches of Articles 12(3) and 15. It ordered the company to reply to the data subject within 30 days and fined it EUR 10,000.

The Garante received a report that a café, run by Rebirth s.r.l., had a non-compliant video surveillance system. The company ignored two requests for information, so the Guardia di Finanza inspected and found 14 working cameras with no information signs and no labour inspectorate authorisation or union agreement. The Garante found the processing unlawful under Articles 5(1)(a) and 13 GDPR and Articles 114 and 157 of the Code, and fined the company EUR 15,000, also ordering publication of the decision.

After a report about a video surveillance system at the company's premises, the Guardia di finanza inspected in November 2021 and found 15 working cameras. Signage was missing in several areas, two cameras exceeded those authorised by the labour authority (authorisation was requested only in 2018 for a 2013 installation), and the three people with access to the footage shared credentials and only one had been instructed. The Garante found the processing unlawful under Articles 5(1)(a) and (c), 13, 29 and 32 GDPR and Article 114 of the Code, rejected the argument that employee consent cured the problem, and fined the company EUR 10,000. The decision is to be published on the Garante's website.

A citizen complained that the municipality of Orte had installed photo-trap cameras with no published notice, signage or information. The Garante found that the municipality had used the devices, if only to test them, without any organisational act, privacy-by-design measures, retention periods or information to the people filmed, and had given its own institutional addresses as its data protection officer's contact details. It declared the processing unlawful, fined the municipality EUR 20,000, ordered it to give the Garante specific contact details for the data protection officer, and ordered publication. The allegation under Article 28 was dismissed. The Viterbo Tribunal later reduced the fine to EUR 5,000 (final judgment 1222/2023); the Garante's published text now shows the reduced amount.

No fine. The Danish DPA reported Danske Bank to the police and recommended DKK 10 million. The case was settled by the prosecution dropping the charge (tiltalefrafald), because the bank was sentenced in another criminal case. In Denmark the data protection authority cannot fine: it reports the case to the police and recommends an amount, and a court sets the fine.

Following press reports, the Belgian DPA investigated the use of thermal cameras and a second-line health check at Brussels Airport to screen passengers for COVID-19 in 2020. The Litigation Chamber found that the airport company and its contractor (the first-aid company running the second-line check) lacked a valid legal basis for the processing of health data, and that the airport company breached transparency duties and the data protection impact assessment rules. It fined the airport company EUR 200,000 and the contractor EUR 20,000, and reprimanded the airport company for finalising its impact assessment late. The decision was later partly annulled (first defendant) and wholly annulled (second defendant) by the Market Court.

The Belgian DPA's Litigation Chamber examined the use of thermal cameras by Charleroi airport to check passengers' temperature during COVID-19. It found there was no adequate legal basis for processing health data, and that transparency and information duties were breached. The DPIA was carried out three months after the processing began and was inadequate. It imposed a EUR 100,000 fine and a reprimand for shortcomings in the processing register. The decision was later partly annulled by the Market Court.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, thermal cameras at Brussels Airport (Zaventem) screened passengers for a temperature above 38°C. Ambuce Rescue Team then carried out a second check, a symptom questionnaire. The Litigation Chamber found that the airports had no valid legal basis for processing this health data, and it also found shortcomings in the information given to travellers and in the impact assessments. It fined Ambuce Rescue Team EUR 20,000, alongside fines of EUR 200,000 on Zaventem and EUR 100,000 on Charleroi. A note on the page says the Market Court later annulled the decision entirely as regards Ambuce Rescue Team.

A customer complained that Piraeus Bank kept sending account-movement alerts (Winbank Alerts) for her debit card to an e-mail address belonging to a third person with the same name, and did not fix it after being told. The bank said the joint account holder had registered an address differing only by a dot, which Gmail treats as identical, and that no breach occurred. The Authority found the bank breached confidentiality (Art. 5(1)(f)) and its duties to notify the breach to the Authority and the data subject (Arts. 33 and 34). It fined the bank EUR 10,000 in total and issued a warning to put in place technical and organisational measures to verify e-mail addresses given for alerts.

A head of department at a municipality complained that the former mayor, now a municipal councillor, sent letters containing her personal data to many recipients, including trade unions, after she chose to be appraised by the new mayor. The former mayor argued that he acted under public authority (Art. 6(1)(e)) and for legitimate interests (Art. 6(1)(f)). The Authority found that sending the letters to the municipal employees' union and to the national federation of municipal employees (POE-OTA) breached the lawfulness principle of Art. 5(1)(a) GDPR. It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 5,000 on him as controller.

A former managing director and employee complained against his ex-employer, which had restored and analysed the mailboxes from his work laptop after dismissal and refused his requests for erasure, restriction and objection. The Litigation Chamber found breaches of lawfulness and minimisation (Art. 5(1)(a), 6(1)(f)), information duties, data subject rights (Arts 15, 17, 18, 21) and Art. 28. It ordered compliance with the complainant's requests, introduction of a policy charter and an end to processing data older than 5 years, and imposed a fine of EUR 7,500. The Market Court later partially annulled the decision.

The Garante issued an urgent interim order against G.O.L. Impresa Sociale S.r.l., the publisher of the online news site Open Online.it. An article published on 31 March 2022 quoted excerpts of messages said to have been exchanged between a school head and a student, dwelling on details of their personal relations, while school authorities were still investigating. The Garante ordered a provisional limitation of any further dissemination of those message contents, online or otherwise, including in any future article by the company or its other publications. It also asked the company to report within 3 days what steps it had taken, and reserved any further decision until the investigation is complete.

Following an Article 60 GDPR cooperation procedure, the Swedish DPA issued a reprimand against a newspaper subscription service which violated Articles 6(1), 12(3) and 21(2) GDPR by failing to stop sending marketing emails despite the data subject's objection.

A former municipal employee asked the municipality for access to all communication in which they were mentioned, including emails and notes sent or signed in their work. After the municipality tried to narrow the request, the employee declined, and the municipality refused the request as manifestly unfounded or excessive under Article 12(5)(b) GDPR. The employee complained to Datatilsynet. Datatilsynet found no grounds to set aside the municipality's assessment, because the material mainly describes the employee's job function, the request covered several years, and the municipality had already disclosed much of the material.

The Hungarian authority examined camera surveillance at the premises of a car repair business, following a report from a company that co-owns the property. It found that cameras in the office/customer waiting room and the kitchen could unjustifiably monitor employees, that the controller relied on employee consent instead of legitimate interest (with no balancing test), and that employees were not properly informed. It ordered the cameras' fields of view changed, the policy and privacy notice amended, and fined the controller HUF 500,000. The decision is to be published in anonymised form.

In an Article 60 GDPR procedure, the Swedish DPA determined that the controller violated Article 32(1) GDPR by failing to provide an appropriate level of security for the internal handling of customers' accounts.

Following a complaint that Condor SA had disclosed employees' and former employees' salary data to unauthorised persons, the Romanian authority investigated. It found unauthorised access to unprotected documents containing personal data, and that the company could not show adequate technical and organisational security measures or staff training. It found an infringement of Article 32(1), (2) and (4) GDPR, imposed a fine of 9,897.4 lei (about EUR 2,000), and ordered two corrective measures.

IMY examined the privacy information that Klarna Bank AB gave customers on its website in spring 2020 (17 March to 26 June 2020). It found that the information was incomplete, misleading or missing on purposes and legal basis for the 'Min Ekonomi' service, recipients such as credit reference agencies, transfers to third countries, retention periods, data subject rights and automated credit decisions. IMY held that Klarna breached Articles 5(1)(a), 5(2), 12(1), 13 and 14 GDPR. It imposed a single joint administrative fine of SEK 7,500,000, treating the information as one and the same processing. Klarna's improvements to the information during the review were counted as mitigating.

A complainant asked the Belgian DPA's Litigation Chamber to force the Federal Public Service Finance to disclose cadastral income data of third-party properties as comparison points for his own property assessment. The chamber dismissed the complaint under Article 95 §1, 3° WOG, on both a technical and a policy ground. It found the requested comparison data were third-party personal data outside the scope of the complainant's Article 15 access right, and that the complaint did not show an GDPR infringement. It also noted the dispute was really a side issue to a tax assessment dispute better handled by a court. No infringement was found and no fine was imposed.

The Danish Data Protection Agency reported the National Genome Center to the police and proposed a fine of DKK 50,000. The centre began processing genetic sequencing data without first consulting the agency, although its own impact assessment showed a high residual risk. The agency had already imposed a temporary ban on further collection in January 2022. The case was settled on 26 April 2024 with a fine order (bødeforelæg) of DKK 50,000.

Romania's data protection authority (ANSPDCP) published a press release on 25 March 2022 about an investigation into Kaufland România SCS, completed in February 2022. The investigation followed a complaint. The authority found that the retailer did not give the complainant a full copy of the store's video surveillance recordings of him, although they were available when he asked, which breached Article 15(3) GDPR. The retailer was fined 9,889.4 lei (about EUR 2,000) and ordered to give the data subject all requested images, with other persons blurred where they could be identified.

An employee of the Caltanissetta provincial health authority complained that a reply concerning his pension position was also sent to his office's certified email and that his access request was not properly answered. The Garante found that the note was made visible through the electronic protocol to other staff, the access request was mishandled, the new DPO's contact details were not communicated through the official procedure, and the authority did not answer the Garante's requests for information. It found breaches of Articles 5, 6, 12, 15 and 37 GDPR, Article 2-ter and Article 157 of the Code, and imposed a fine of EUR 6,000 plus publication of the decision. No further corrective measures were ordered since the conduct had ceased.

The Municipality of Genoa's local police used a fines-management platform (ScatWeb) supplied by Brav s.r.l., which acted as processor. Unauthorised people accessed it because officers' first-access passwords (their badge numbers) were never changed and the access URL was circulated. The Garante found that Brav had not ensured password quality or forced a change at first login, left the service available over insecure http, and lacked server logs with IP addresses for the breach period. It declared the processing unlawful under Articles 5(1)(f) and 32 GDPR and fined Brav EUR 10,000, with publication of the decision. No corrective measure was imposed on the Municipality.

The Italian DPA fined Uber a total of €4,240,000 for violations relating to 1,500,000 data subjects in Italy, including lack of transparency and consent and failure to notify the DPA of a personal data breach.

The Polish DPA fined an individual who was the plenipotentiary of a group of citizens initiating a local referendum to recall a municipal council. The DPA had asked him, in a separate proceeding, for information about signature collection and the destruction of signature cards, and he received two written requests but did not answer either. The DPA found breaches of Article 31 and Article 58(1)(e) GDPR, treated the Article 58(1)(e) breach as the most serious, and imposed a fine of PLN 2,285 (stated as EUR 500). The decision is marked as final (prawomocna).

The Finnish DPA issued a reprimand against the Ministry of Foreign Affairs for the late notification of a data breach to both the DPA and the data subjects under Articles 33 and 34 GDPR. The DPA held that although controllers can investigate potential data breaches before the 72-hour time limit in Article 33 GDPR starts running, the Ministry failed to do so after it had concluded its investigation, without providing justified reasons for the delay.

Three volunteers who had signed up for a municipal face-mask distribution complained that a municipal alderman used the e-mail addresses they had sent to the general municipal mailbox to contact them personally from her professional address. The Litigation Chamber found the municipality was the controller and that the lawful basis was the performance of a task in the public interest (Art. 6(1)(e)). It found the alderman acted within the original purpose, used blind carbon copy so addresses were not visible to each other, and deleted the addresses after the distribution. It therefore found no infringement of the GDPR and dismissed the complaint.

An employee complained that her manager had disclosed to her whole department (51 recipients), by email, that she was undergoing fertility treatment, in order to explain her work restrictions. The municipality said the disclosure rested on a misunderstood consent given during a phone call, and later admitted that this consent was not valid. The Danish DPA found that telling colleagues the reason for the restrictions was not necessary, so the disclosure breached the data minimisation principle in Article 5(1)(c) GDPR. Given the confidential nature of the data and the size of the group it was shared with, it issued a severe criticism (reprimand) and no fine. The municipality had offered the complainant compensation.

A complainant asked Klarna Bank AB for erasure of her personal data under Article 17 GDPR on 18 November 2020. Klarna verified her identity on 25 November 2020 and completed the erasure on 24 January 2021, but only told her of the delay and the up-to-90-day period on that date. IMY held that the request was not handled without undue delay under Article 12(3) GDPR, but considered the infringement minor, due to a single human error affecting one person, and issued a reprimand instead of a fine.

The Deputy Data Protection Ombudsman examined the City of Oulu's social services, which required prospective foster and support family carers to use their right of access to obtain their own police records and show the results to the city. The city said it was in a legal gap and had been doing this for a long time. The decision found that the city processed personal data, including criminal offence data, without a lawful basis, in breach of Articles 6(1) and 10 GDPR. The city issued a reprimand under Article 58(2)(b) and noted that it would stop the practice.

A former customer asked a company to delete his account and personal data after moving. The company deleted the address he used to send the request, but kept his old email address in a separate prospect database and kept sending him marketing email. It also did not reply within one month about what it had done with the request. The Litigation Chamber found a partial breach of the right to erasure (Article 17(1)) and a breach of the one-month deadline to inform about measures taken (Article 12(3)). It did not find a breach of the access rules, and it imposed a reprimand rather than a fine.

The Danish DPA issued a warning against a company related to its intended use of a facial recognition system. The DPA held that the company may only process biometric data in this way with the data subjects' consent under Article 9(2)(a) GDPR.

The Norwegian DPA fined a company €9,775 for unlawfully enabling automatic forwarding of an employee's emails in violation of Article 6(1)(f), for lack of information as per Article 13, failure to assess their objection as per Article 21, and required them to improve internals controls for employee emails as per Article 24 GDPR.

The Irish DPC opened an own-volition inquiry into Meta Platforms Ireland Limited (then Facebook Ireland Limited) after twelve personal data breaches were notified to it in 2018. The DPC found that the company failed to have systems and procedures to demonstrate its technical and organisational security measures, an infringement of Article 5(2) GDPR, and also found an infringement of Article 24(1) GDPR. Only the Article 5(2) infringement was fined, with a fine of EUR 17 million; no order was made because the company's voluntary changes made it unnecessary.

The Irish DPC ran an own-volition inquiry into Bank of Ireland after a series of personal data breach notifications about inaccurate data uploaded to the Central Credit Register. It found the bank infringed Articles 33 (late or imprecise notification to the DPC), 34 (late communication to affected customers) and 32 (inadequate technical and organisational measures). The DPC issued a reprimand, ordered the bank to implement a procedure and confirm compliance within 90 days, and imposed several fines totalling EUR 463,000.

The Icelandic DPA reprimanded a primary school for mistakenly including the medical data of a student in emails sent to the parents of other students when handling a bullying case, in violation of Articles 9, 5(1)(f), 24, 25 and 32 GDPR.

The Belgian DPA held that, under the GDPR, direct marketing via email may not require the data subject's consent. However, it is still necessary to inform the data subject pursuant to Article 14 GDPR at the latest at the time of initial contact.

The Belgian DPA held that a car dealership violated Articles 12 and 15 GDPR by not complying with an access request, as well as Articles 5(1)(f), 5(2), 24 and 32 GDPR due to a lack security measures which led to a data breach.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation of Briza Land S.R.L. on 24 February 2022 after a complaint from a person unhappy with the reply to their access request. It found that the company had not given the complainant all the information about the processing of their data, such as the data processed, its source and its recipients, which breaches Article 15 GDPR. The company was fined RON 9,892.6, stated to be the equivalent of EUR 2,000. It was also ordered to give the complainant all the information within 5 working days of receiving the report.

The Tuscany Centre local health authority notified the Garante of two data breaches: a medical record copy handed to the wrong person, and two radiology reports mailed to each other's patients by mistake. The Garante joined the two proceedings and found that health data were disclosed to third parties without a legal basis, in breach of Articles 5(1)(a) and (f), 9 and 32 GDPR. Because the conduct had exhausted its effects and corrective measures were already in place, it imposed no corrective orders. It fined the authority EUR 10,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

A former employee of a regional environmental agency complained that the agency published in full, without anonymisation and indexed by search engines, a resolution approving a union conciliation settlement. It also referred to a criminal case in which he was acquitted. The Garante found that the agency had no legal basis for disseminating the data online, including data on criminal proceedings, and that this breached Articles 5, 6 and 10 GDPR and Articles 2-ter and 2-octies of the Code. It fined the agency EUR 8,000 and ordered publication of the decision on the Garante's website.

The health authority ASST di Lodi notified a personal data breach: an employee of its public relations office disclosed a patient's health data to a relative who was not the person the patient had designated. The Garante found that the disclosure had no legal basis and breached the ban on processing health data and the security and integrity principles. Taking into account that the case was isolated, involved one recipient, was notified and handled cooperatively, with training and disciplinary measures already taken, it imposed a fine of EUR 1,000 and ordered publication of the decision. No corrective orders were imposed.

A complainant had earlier asked a shipyard company to erase his data and got no answer; in decision n. 166 of 29 April 2021 the Garante fined it and ordered it to reply to him within 60 days. The company neither complied nor answered the Garante's information request, so the Guardia di finanza inspected it in October 2021, and only then did the company write to the complainant. The Garante found a breach of the duty to comply with a corrective order (Art. 83(6) GDPR) and of Art. 157 of the Italian Code (failure to answer information requests). It imposed a single fine of EUR 10,000 and ordered publication of the decision. A note says the court appeal was later extinguished.

The UK DPA fined law firm €116,784.27 (GBP 98,000) for contravening Article 5(1)(f) and Article 32 GDPR by "failing to process personal data in a manner that ensured appropriate security of the personal data.”

In an Article 60 GDPR procedure, the Estonian DPA issued a warning to a controller. Among other things, the data subject was not able to create a user account without consenting to direct marketing in violation of Article 7(2) GDPR.

An employee teacher who gave online lessons via Zoom complained that her employer, who ran a tutoring centre, watched her lessons continuously, despite her explicit objections. The employer argued that the monitoring was needed for technical quality and parental satisfaction, and claimed implied or later consent. The Authority found breaches of the lawfulness, transparency and accountability principles, of the duty to inform under Article 13, and that the right to object was not honoured. It imposed a fine of EUR 2,000.

This is a press release announcing two fines, totalling HRK 1.6 million. Only the second one matches this Fino entry. A retail chain notified the Agency of a personal data breach: employees had filmed the video surveillance monitor with their mobile phones, and the footage spread on social media and in the media. The Agency found that the chain had taken some organisational steps, such as training, internal rules and confidentiality statements, but not adequate technical and organisational measures, either before or after the incident. It also did not regularly test the effectiveness of its measures. The Agency imposed an administrative fine of HRK 675,000 for breaching Article 32 GDPR.

A complainant objected that Harpa, buying tickets through the Tix online ticketing system, required his national identification number (kennitala) or date of birth. Persónuvernd found this collection was not necessary to fulfil the contract, since tickets could be delivered using other identifiers, and that customers were not told registration was optional. Harpa breached the lawfulness, data minimisation and transparency principles, the legal basis rules and the national ID number provision. It was ordered to stop collecting and to delete the data already collected, and fined ISK 1,000,000. The fine was reduced because Harpa could not change its practice once Covid rules required registration and it acted in good faith, but increased somewhat by its poor cooperation.

The Icelandic DPA reprimanded a university for not providing students adequate information regarding the processing of their personal data when remotely monitoring exams taken at home via Zoom due to the COVID19 pandemic, in violation of Articles 5(1)(f) and 32 GDPR.

The Basque DPA held that Articles 6(1)(c) and 6(1)(e) GDPR supplied a legal basis for a local police force to include personal data in files sent to the Chief of the Police, the Mayor’s Office, and the Councilman of Citizen Security. It is still assessing whether this practice complies with the principle of data minimisation.

Royal Mail reported that, on 27 April 2021, a manual routing error caused its 'War of the Roses' reminder marketing email to be sent to 215,202 customers who had opted out of marketing. Of these, 213,191 were delivered. The Commissioner found that Royal Mail had no valid consent for these messages, that it could not rely on the soft opt-in for guest customers, and that the contravention was serious and negligent. A penalty of £20,000 was imposed under the Data Protection Act 1998 for breach of regulation 22 PECR, with a 20% early payment discount.

The Danish Agency for Digitisation notified a personal data breach after it mistakenly gave 26 curators access to the digital mailboxes of the wrong companies, apparently because the company CVR-number lines on a manually prepared list were shifted. The agency had not previously seen errors in this list and relied on the absence of past human errors as its security. The Danish DPA found that this was not an appropriate security level under Article 32(1) GDPR and issued a reprimand (kritik), with no fine. It noted the agency had introduced a four-eyes check on the lists afterwards.

In September 2020 attackers gained unauthorised access to the email accounts of a number of members of parliament and staff of the Norwegian Parliament, and data including bank details, national ID numbers and health data may have been exposed from 13 accounts. Datatilsynet found that Parliament had not implemented suitable technical and organisational measures, in particular two-factor authentication, even though its own risk analysis from March 2020 had identified the lack of it as high risk. It rejected Parliament's arguments about the pandemic and the lack of instruction authority over MPs and party staff. It imposed an administrative fine of NOK 2,000,000 under Articles 32(1)(b) and (d) and 5(1)(f). The decision could be appealed by 15 August 2022.

In an Article 60 GDPR procedure, the DPA of Malta reprimanded a controller pursuant of Article 58(2)(b) GDPR) for requiring an ID-photo as identification method to exercise an access request. The DPA also ordered the controller to comply with the request pursuant of Article 58(2)(d) GDPR.

The Danish DPA opened an own-initiative case after learning in March 2021 that a user logging into e-Boks Express with a NemID keycard could reach another user's profile. A configuration error by Nets in the NemID user validation exposed other companies' details, the titles and dispatch times of sent documents. The DPA found that e-Boks had not tested all relevant login scenarios, so it had not implemented appropriate security under Article 32(1). It also found a personal data breach under Article 4(12). The outcome was criticism (a reprimand), with no fine.

The Bremen data protection authority fined the housing company BREBAU GmbH about EUR 1.9 million under Article 83 GDPR. The company had processed more than 9,500 data items about prospective tenants without any legal basis, including hair style, body odour and personal appearance. More than half of the cases involved specially protected data such as skin colour, ethnic origin, religion, sexual orientation and health. The company also deliberately frustrated data subjects' requests for transparency. The authority said a much higher fine would have been appropriate, but reduced it considerably because of the company's full cooperation, its efforts to limit damage and clarify the facts, and its steps to prevent repetition.

The Danish Data Protection Agency carried out a written supervision of Høje-Taastrup Municipality's access rights to its file systems in 2021. It found that the municipality had 12 AD groups with access to the LOIS database, which holds national identification numbers, but had no guidelines or objective criteria for joining those groups. The municipality could not document an assessment of employees' work-related need for access, and 410 people had AD access. The Agency found a violation of Article 32(1) GDPR and expressed criticism, without a fine, and recommended that the municipality describe objectively the functions that justify access and have a manager verify the need.

A subscriber asked a telecom provider to remove their name, address and phone number from its public online directory, but a technical error and an administrative mistake meant the data stayed online for years. The provider could not show that the subscriber had consented to publication, and it wrongly logged the phone requests as complaints. The authority found violations of Articles 17(1)(b), 5(2), 6(1) and 12(2) GDPR and fined the provider HUF 5,000,000. The erasure request itself was rejected as moot because the data had been deleted during the proceedings.

The Hungarian authority examined, on its own initiative, a national online and paper petition against compulsory vaccination run by an association and its former representative. It found that they collected personal data, including special-category data, without a legal basis, that the purpose was unclear, that the information given to signatories was inadequate and misleading about who the controller was, and that they could not demonstrate compliance. It ordered deletion of the data collected online, confirmatory consent or deletion for the paper sheets, and a stop to further collection. It fined each respondent HUF 3,000,000, HUF 6,000,000 in total. The authority treated the real purpose as building a sympathiser database, and noted that the petition had about 58,000 supporting signatures.

The Austrian DPA (DSB) held that a controller unlawfully relied on Article 6(1)(f) GDPR and Article 6(1)(c) GDPR as legal bases for processing of personal data obtained from GPS-tracking devices installed on company vehicles used by its employees.

In an Article 60 GDPR procedure, the DPA of Malta reprimanded a controller (Article 58(2)(b) GDPR) for requesting the data subject to sign an agreement in order to process his erasure request. The controller also had to reply to the request (Article 58(2)(d) GDPR).

The Norwegian DPA intends to fine a company €29,376 for monitoring and accessing a prior employee's emails without a legal basis in Article 6(1)(f) GDPR, for lack of information as per Article 13, failure to assess their objection as per Article 21, and lack of technical and organisational measures as per Article 24.

The Dutch DPA investigated how the Minister of Foreign Affairs handles Schengen visa applications in the NVIS system. It found that the security plan was missing, physical protection was insufficient, access rights, logging and incident procedures were incomplete, and applicants were not adequately told who receives their data. It fined the Minister EUR 565,000 for breaching Articles 32(1) and 13(1)(e) GDPR. It also imposed penalty-payment orders to end the continuing violations, with deadlines of 24 October 2022 (security) and 24 March 2022 (information). The press release adds that by May 2023 the information duty was met in time, while the security measures came late and a EUR 50,000 penalty payment was due.
The Italian DPA held that the Bank of Italy violated Articles 5 and 6 GDPR by unlawfully disclosing personal information in the context of a recruitment procedure.

The Romanian authority investigated a law firm after a complaint from a client whose personal data was disclosed without consent or prior information. The firm posted a letter the client had received from a public institution in a WhatsApp group used by lawyers of a bar association, with 247 members. The authority found breaches of Article 5(1)(a), (b), (c), (f), Article 5(2) and Article 6 GDPR. It fined the firm 4,946 lei, equivalent to EUR 1,000, and imposed two corrective measures: notifying group members so the address is deleted, and ensuring compliant handling of clients' data, including regular staff training.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation into IAMSAT Muntenia SA after a complaint from a former employee. The company had not shown it informed employees about video surveillance introduced in mid-2020, and it did not answer the complainant's objection request within the legal deadline. Two fines were imposed (EUR 2,000 and EUR 1,000, total EUR 3,000), plus two corrective measures requiring full information to employees and a reply to the complainant.

The Estonian Data Protection Inspectorate handled three complaints from individuals in Latvia and Poland, transmitted through the IMI system, about a mobile app operator's handling of access, erasure and identity-verification requests. The operator had responded to the requests, deleted the accounts, and cooperated with the inspectorate, but the processing was found not transparent enough. The inspectorate found a breach of Article 5(1)(a) GDPR and issued a reprimand, with no fine. It held that asking for an ID card to verify identity was permitted under Article 12(6), but that the operator should have explained why and on what legal basis it was needed.

The Danish DPA (Datatilsynet) held that the Capital Region of Denmark violated Article 32(1) GDPR for negligence related to its health platform's software updates, which led to two separate data breaches involving 4,459 data subjects' health data.

A driver involved in a traffic accident in the Heraklion port asked the port authority for access to its CCTV footage of the accident. The authority refused, citing an ongoing GDPR compliance process, and ignored two follow-up requests. Before the HDPA it claimed the footage had already been deleted after 6 days, but the HDPA found the footage was still held when the first request was made. The HDPA found a breach of the right of access (Art. 15(1) with Art. 12(1),(2) GDPR) and fined the port authority EUR 30,000.
The Austrian DPA found that the Minister of Finances implementing instructions from a a parliamentary anti corruption committee falls within the scope of the GDPR.

The ICO issued The Money Hive Limited, a short-term payday loan lender and broker, with a monetary penalty of £50,000 for a serious contravention of Regulation 22 of PECR. The company sent unsolicited marketing texts promoting loan products to people who had applied for loans on its websites, including links to third-party brokers. The notice states that a total of 752,425 text messages were received by subscribers. A 20% reduction to £40,000 applies if the penalty is paid early.

A trade union complained that Amazon Road Transport Spain required self-employed delivery drivers applying to its transport programme to provide a certificate of no criminal record. The AEPD found this processed criminal-conviction data without a legal basis under Article 6(1) GDPR read with Article 10 GDPR and Article 10 LOPDGDD, and fined the company EUR 2,000,000. It found no infringement of Article 7 (consent) or Article 49.1 (international transfers), and ordered the company to bring its processing and information to data subjects into line within one month.

A person who inherited from a deceased relative received a payment demand from a debt-collection company for a claim that was time-barred and exceeded the estate. The person asked by phone for their data to be deleted, but the company did not handle the request properly. The Hungarian authority found breaches of the principles of lawfulness, fairness, transparency and purpose limitation, accountability, the lawful basis, and the rules on data subject requests and information. It imposed a fine of HUF 10,000,000 ex officio, stressing repeated earlier violations by the same company. It dismissed the request for publication, terminated the part on the period before 25 May 2018 and on erasure, and ordered HUF 10,000 paid to the complainant for exceeding the procedural deadline.
The French DPA held that a French online respondent violated Chapter V of the GDPR by using Google Analytics, which led to unlawful transfers of personal data to Google LLC in the U.S.

A former executive of Costampress S.p.A. complained that after he was dismissed the company kept his work email account, did not give him back his company phone number which had also been used privately, and blocked and examined his company laptop, including private WhatsApp chats. The Garante found the company's processing unlawful for breaching the fairness principle and the transparency and information duties (Arts. 5(1)(a), 12 and 13 GDPR). Other alleged breaches (Arts. 5(1)(c), 6 and 20) were dropped. It fined the company EUR 10,000 and ordered publication of the decision on the Garante's website.

The Italian Garante investigated Clearview AI, a US facial recognition company that scrapes images from the web and builds biometric data, after press reports, complaints and reports from privacy groups. It rejected the company's argument that the GDPR does not apply and found breaches of the processing principles, legal basis, special-category rules, transparency, access rights and the duty to appoint an EU representative. It banned further collection and processing of data of people in Italy, ordered deletion of that data, ordered appointment of a representative, and fined the company EUR 20 million, the maximum under Art. 83(5). The Art. 22 allegation was not upheld.

A regional health service company (ASST) notified the Garante of a personal data breach: a lab result for a diagnostic test was handed to a patient who was not the person it belonged to. The Garante found the processing unlawful because health data was disclosed to a third party without a valid legal basis, breaching the integrity and confidentiality principle and Article 9. It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 3,500 and ordered publication of the decision on its website.

The Region of Tuscany notified a personal data breach in which the results and personal data of about 3,600 candidates in a public recruitment competition were exposed online for about an hour. Its processor, Scanshare, uploaded the data without access authentication, and a web link was mistakenly emailed to a candidate and then shared in a WhatsApp group. The Garante held the Region responsible as controller despite the processor's main fault, found breaches of Articles 5 and 6 GDPR and Article 2-ter of the Code, and fined it EUR 10,000. It ordered publication of the decision and saw no need for further corrective measures.

Scanshare S.r.l., processor for the Regione Toscana's public recruitment competition, uploaded candidates' results to a web server without access authentication. A link sent by mistake to a candidate matched the upload folder, so data of about 3,600 candidates became accessible and was shared in a WhatsApp group. The Garante found that Scanshare had not applied adequate security measures (Art. 32) and had used a hosting provider (Hostinger) without the controller's prior written authorisation (Art. 28(2)). It fined the company EUR 10,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

A complainant was named in a full municipal resolution (a revocation of an inter-municipal police officer transfer) published on the council's online notice board and left visible in the transparency section beyond the 15-day publication period. The resolution also described the complainant's criminal complaints against a colleague. The Garante found the online dissemination of the complainant's personal data unlawful under Articles 5(1)(a) and (c) and 6 GDPR and Article 2-ter of the Italian Privacy Code (text before DL 139/2021). It fined the municipality EUR 2,000 and ordered publication of the decision on the Garante's website.

A complainant, listed years earlier in an online directory of shiatsu operators, repeatedly asked for his data to be deleted but received no answer. The Garante found that the company publishing the portal was the controller and was responsible for the failure to erase and to reply, even though the site was run by its majority shareholder who no longer had access. The company also did not answer the Garante's request for information, but no separate fine was imposed for that. The site was taken offline only after the Garante intervened, so no corrective order was needed, and a fine of EUR 5,000 was imposed with publication of the decision.

A property owner complained that a real estate agency kept phoning him with promotions and ignored his access and erasure request sent by certified email. The agency had taken his number from public websites and a Google search, without consent or another legal basis, and had not given him the Article 14 information. It also answered the Garante's information requests late and inadequately. The Garante declared the processing unlawful, restricted the processing of web-sourced data without consent, ordered procedures for handling data subject rights and for giving information, and fined the company EUR 5,000, with publication of the decision.

The Authority opened an ex officio procedure against Budapest Bank over its AI-based analysis of recorded customer service calls, which assessed the emotional state of callers and employees and ranked calls for call-backs and quality control. It found breaches of the principles of purpose limitation and lawfulness, legal basis, transparency, the right to object, accountability and data protection by design and default. The bank was ordered to bring the practice into line, stop analysing emotions and guarantee data subject rights, including adequate information to employees. A fine of HUF 250,000,000 was imposed, taking into account the bank's turnover of HUF 81 billion and the seriousness and long duration of the infringement.

The ICO issued Tempcover Ltd, a UK motor insurance provider, with a monetary penalty of £85,000 under the Data Protection Act 1998 for a serious contravention of regulation 22 of PECR. Between May 2019 and May 2020 subscribers who had requested insurance quotes received about 29.97 million unsolicited direct marketing messages (SMS and email) from Tempcover. It relied on consent bundled into its terms and conditions and on legitimate interest, and could not use the soft opt-in because it gave no simple way to refuse marketing when the data was collected. The notice also records that the penalty would be reduced by 20% to £68,000 if paid early.

A former online-casino customer complained that a law firm, acting for a casino company in a civil claim he had brought, used his personal data that a sister company had passed on to that casino company. The authority found the processing justified: the law firm had a legitimate interest in presenting its client's defence, and the processing was covered by Article 6(1)(f) read with Article 9(2)(f) GDPR. The complaint was dismissed, and no fine was imposed.

A complainant objected to TV 2 and its law firm Norrbom Vinding processing information about him, including his sexual life, during an investigation of workplace culture and alleged harassment. The Danish DPA (decided with the Data Council because it was a principle case) found that TV 2 had a legitimate interest under Art. 6(1)(f) and that the sexual-life information could be processed under Art. 9(2)(f) for legal claims, so it did not criticise that processing. It did find that the collection did not have the required Art. 9 basis and was not in line with Art. 25 and Art. 5, and that the complainant was not informed as required by Arts. 12 and 14. The result was a serious criticism (reprimand); no fine was imposed.

The Norwegian DPA fined a municipality €29,880 for publishing a confidential document with a pupil's sensitive personal data, including potential diagnoses such as ADHD, in breach of Articles 32(1)(b), 6, and 5 GDPR.

The Belgian DPA found that IAB Europe's Transparency and Consent Framework (TCF), used in online real-time bidding for personalised advertising, breaches several GDPR provisions. The Litigation Chamber held IAB Europe responsible as a controller for the TC String that records users' consent preferences. It imposed a EUR 250,000 fine and ordered corrective measures, including a valid legal basis for the TCF and a ban on legitimate interest as a basis for processing by participants, with an action plan due within two months. The press release says the decision can be appealed, and later updates report appeals to the Market Court.

The municipality published a document on its public mail journal website in which 10 of 21 attachments contained confidential special-category data about a pupil, because the attachments were not marked as exempt. A journalist noticed it and four different IP addresses accessed the document. The Datatilsynet found a lack of appropriate security measures (no routines for follow-up checks of published documents) and publication without a legal basis. It imposed an administrative fine of NOK 300,000 after lowering the culpability from grossly negligent to negligent following the municipality's reply.

The CNPD opened an investigation into Société A, a café operator, and visited its premises on 29 January 2020, finding eleven fixed cameras, ten inside and one outside facing the street, plus some dummy cameras. The restricted committee found that the cameras filmed workstations, consumption areas and the public road, breaching the data minimisation principle, and that the video surveillance notices did not meet the transparency requirements of Article 13 GDPR. It imposed a single administrative fine of EUR 1,000 and ordered the company to bring its processing into compliance within two months, including removing or refocusing certain cameras and providing full Article 13 information to staff and third parties.

The Romanian data protection authority finished an investigation of SC Grupex 2000 SRL on 7 January 2022. It found the company had unlawfully processed the personal data of institutionalised patients by publishing a video showing them on its website. The company was fined RON 4,943.60 (about EUR 1,000) and ordered to bring its processing into line with the GDPR through appropriate technical and organisational measures. The investigation began after referrals from a County Directorate for Social Assistance and Child Protection.

The Norwegian DPA intends to fine a private investigation company €5,000 for unlawfully credit rating the former boyfriend of a client and for not adhering to the accountability principle as per Article 5(2) GDPR, cf. Article 24, and also requires them to implement internal controls for their credit rating process.

The Finnish DPA held that a parking services provider violated Article 5(1)(c) and Article 25 GDPR because, in cases where a technical failure occurred with the payment machine, data subjects were prompted to provide their phone number to receive the receipt via SMS, and were not adequately informed that they could also opt for a printed copy without having to provide their phone number.

A user asked the online marketplace DBA to delete his profile and the personal data attached to it, including e-mail, name and CPR number. DBA refused, saying it had received three independent buyer complaints about him and needed to keep the data to block him from creating new profiles, and it had blocked him from eight e-mail addresses before. The Danish regulator found that DBA could not rely on vital interests but that the correct basis was legitimate interests under Article 6(1)(f), which outweighed the user's interest, so DBA was not obliged to erase the data under Article 17(1). It also found no breach of storage limitation under Article 5(1)(e), since data is deleted automatically after 24 months of inactivity.
The UK DPA (ICO) fined Home2sense €240,317.08 (GBP 200,000) for making unsolicited direct marketing calls in violation of Regulation 21 and 24 PECR.
The German Federal DPA issued a decision specifying which data a telecommunications and internet company should provide to a data subject when handling an access request under Article 15 GDPR.

After a study on the political origin of tweets about a French political affair was published, and raw data files with personal data were put online, many people complained to the Belgian DPA. The Chamber found breaches of the GDPR for processing 2, including data minimisation (5(1)(c)), missing legal basis (6(1)(f)), processing of sensitive data without an exception (9(1)), missing transparency (12 and 14) and inadequate security (32). It dismissed the complaints under Articles 28 and 30. The second respondent, a researcher, received a reprimand and a EUR 1,200 fine.

A Belgian non-profit fighting disinformation and one of its volunteers published online the raw Twitter data, including personal data of many users, behind a study of tweets on a French political controversy. Over 240 people complained to the Belgian and French authorities. The Litigation Chamber, as lead authority, found that there was no valid legal basis, that the data were not minimised or secured, that sensitive data (political opinions, sexual orientation) were included, and that data subjects were not informed. It rejected the journalistic exception. It imposed a reprimand and a fine of EUR 2,700 on the association and a reprimand and a fine of EUR 1,200 on the individual, and dropped the complaints under Articles 28 and 30.

COSMOTE notified the authority of a personal data breach in September 2020. An attacker used a stolen administrator password to get into an OTE-hosted system and exfiltrated a 30 GB file of call data from COSMOTE's Big Data system. The data covered millions of subscribers and users of other providers. After a hearing of both COSMOTE and OTE, the authority found many infringements by COSMOTE.
