These concerned transparency, the data protection impact assessment, data protection by design (anonymisation), the joint-controller/processor arrangements with OTE, the legality of processing and security under the national e-privacy law. It also found an Article 32 GDPR security failure by OTE. COSMOTE received GDPR fines totalling EUR 5,850,000 plus EUR 150,000 under the old law 2472/1997, and OTE received EUR 3,250,000.

COSMOTE notified the Authority of a breach in which a hacker used an OTE administrator's password, leaked through a LinkedIn breach, to get into OTE infrastructure. From there the hacker queried COSMOTE's Big Data system and exfiltrated a 30 GB file of subscriber call data covering 1-5 September 2020. After a hearing of both companies, the Authority found OTE in breach of Article 32 GDPR for inadequate security measures. It found COSMOTE in breach of several GDPR provisions (Articles 35(7), 5(1)(a) with 13 and 14, 25(1), 5(2) with 26 and 28) and of the national e-privacy law 3471/2006 (Articles 5, 6 and 12(1)). COSMOTE received fines totalling EUR 5,850,000 under the GDPR plus EUR 150,000 under the old law 2472/1997, and orders to stop processing and destroy data. OTE was fined EUR 3,250,000.

After a report from a Carabinieri station, the Florence municipal police inspected a private club on 22 June 2020 and found nine cameras (six inside, three outside) with no information signage. Two outdoor cameras were aimed at the pavement, the road and, in one case, the facade of a nearby Carabinieri barracks. The club did not send any defence submissions. The Garante found breaches of Article 5(1)(a) and (c) GDPR (lawfulness, transparency and minimisation) and of Article 13 (information duty). It ordered the club to post signage and limit the cameras to its own premises, imposed a fine of EUR 2,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

A data subject complained that TSM gave an incomplete reply to his access, erasure and objection requests after he received contract forms in its name for a professional training course. TSM only said it had deleted his data, gave no information on the processing, did not confirm the objection, and ignored two requests for information from the Garante. The forms also carried no privacy notice. The Garante found breaches of Articles 13, 15 and 21 GDPR and of Articles 157 and 166(2) of the Code, issued a warning, ordered TSM to answer the complainant, banned further processing of his data and fined TSM EUR 40,000. A note at the top says the appeal ended with a final judgment favourable to the company by the Tribunal of Rome in January 2023.

A person who had taken part in a public competition in 2019 complained that a search result linked to his name pointed to a document published by a local authority listing the candidates admitted and not admitted to the oral exam, with their scores. Google refused to delist it. The Garante held that the competition had ended, that publishing intermediate results had no specific public interest, and that the continued disclosure was disproportionate. It upheld the complaint and ordered Google to delist the URL from name searches within twenty days. It also decided to note the measure in its internal register, without precedent value for future proceedings under Article 83(2).

IMY opened an investigation after the Uppsala regional board reported a personal data incident. The board had sent Excel files with patient data, including health data and personal identity numbers, by internal email. Only the transport was encrypted, not the file contents, and this went against the region's own guidelines. IMY found a breach of Article 32(1) GDPR for the period 25 May 2018 to 7 May 2019 and imposed an administrative fine of SEK 300,000.

After the Uppsala region reported a personal data incident, IMY examined how Akademiska sjukhuset emailed patient data to patients and referring hospitals abroad. Health data was sent by email that was not reliably encrypted, because the hospital relied on opportunistic TLS, and medical records were also stored in Outlook. This went against the region's own guidelines. IMY found breaches of Articles 5(1)(f) and 32(1) between 25 May 2018 and 7 May 2019 and imposed an administrative fine of SEK 1,600,000 on the hospital board.

A small Irish credit union accidentally left member enquiry reports in a directors' area of its website that became searchable online for about a week in November 2018, exposing data of 76 members, 34 of them children. It notified the breach, and the DPC opened an own-volition inquiry. The DPC found infringements of the security obligations (Articles 5(1)(f) and 32(1)), and also of Articles 24, 28 and 30(1). It issued a reprimand and a single fine of EUR 5,000, calculated on the Article 5(1)(f) infringement, noting the credit union's prompt reaction and cooperation but also its negligence.

A benefit recipient complained that the Center for Social Welfare disclosed his personal data to Croatian Post, whose courier asked for his ID when delivering his minimum guaranteed benefit payment by post. The Agency found that the Center sent the payment by postal money order, that Croatian Post checked identity under its general terms, and that the data passed were no more than necessary. The request was rejected as unfounded, with no fine or order.

The Irish DPC found no personal data breach pursuant to Article 32 GDPR when the Personal Injuries Assessment Board (PIAB) unexpectedly received an unencrypted USB storage device in a ripped envelope by ordinary post.

The Polish data protection authority opened proceedings on its own initiative after an energy and gas seller notified a personal data breach. During a change to its IT environment made by its processor, a copy of a customer database sat on a server without proper security and was copied by unauthorised people, exposing the data of more than 95,000 customers. The authority found that the controller had not implemented adequate technical and organisational measures and had not verified its processor, and fined it PLN 4,911,732. The processor was fined PLN 250,135 for failing to secure the data. The part of the case on the duty to notify data subjects (Art. 34) was discontinued because the controller notified them during the proceedings.
The Belgian DPA issued a reprimand against a website owner for violating Article 12 and Article 13 GDPR and ordered them to comply with their processing register.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation in December 2021 into Kaufland România SCS after a data subject complained that the company had not given a full copy of CCTV recordings covering a given time slot while the person was in the store. The authority found that the controller had to provide the video of the data subject, blurring images of other people where needed, and had not provided it completely. This breached the right of access under Article 15(3) GDPR. The controller received a contravention fine of 14,846.4 lei (about EUR 3,000).

The Estonian DPA held that the legal basis for transferring a data subject's debt data to a third party was legitimate interest, not contractual necessity. The DPA also reprimanded the controller for failing to reply to an access request within one month.

A bank notified the Polish authority of a breach: a former employee still had access to the ZUS electronic services platform and could view the personal data, including sick-leave (health) data, of about 10,500 employees. The bank decided not to inform the employees, arguing that the former employee had already had broad access while employed. The President of UODO found a violation of Article 34(1) GDPR because the data subjects were not notified without undue delay despite high risk. He imposed a fine of PLN 545,748 (about EUR 120,000) and ordered the bank to notify all affected employees within 3 days with the information required by Article 34(2).

The ICO issued a monetary penalty notice to Energy Suite Limited, a company selling energy-saving grant schemes, for a serious contravention of regulation 21 of PECR. Between 1 March and 13 November 2020 the company made unsolicited direct marketing calls to at least 1,246 numbers registered with the Telephone Preference Service, and relied on purchased lead data without proper checks. The Commissioner imposed a penalty of £2,000, with a 20% early-payment discount to £1,600 if paid by 16 February 2022.

The Slovenian Information Commissioner, acting ex officio in an inspection supervision case, examined how an employer, whose name is redacted in the text, informed staff about colleagues who had contracted COVID-19. The employer sent staff e-mails naming the infected employees. The Commissioner found that naming the individuals was unlawful and breached the data minimisation principle in Article 5(1)(c) GDPR, since the same warning could have been given without names, for example by blind copy. The Commissioner ordered the employer to stop naming infected employees, to take measures so this does not recur, and to comply within 15 days and report within 5 days after. No fine was imposed, and the decision is final in the administrative procedure, with an administrative dispute possible.

The Spanish DPA carried out an investigation in response to a claim against Grindr by a human rights NGO, and found no violations of GDPR as to consent regarding processing of personal data for advertisement purposes or the processing of special categories of personal data.

Under Article 60 GDPR the Belgian DPA (LSA) and other concerned authorities ordered a controller to comply with a data subject's request to erasure according to Article 58(2)(c) GDPR, because it did not comply with the request.

In April 2020 the Maltese Commissioner learned of a security incident at C-Planet (IT Solutions) Ltd and opened an investigation. He found that the company processed personal and special-category data unlawfully and failed to apply appropriate security measures. It also failed to notify the breach to the authority in time and to inform the affected data subjects. He imposed a fine of EUR 65,000 and ordered erasure of the unlawfully processed data. The company cooperated fully.

A complainant reported that the partnership published, on Facebook and Instagram, images of her and her partner with comments intended to discredit them. The AEPD found the publication had no legal basis under Article 6(1) GDPR and noted the partnership did not answer the AEPD's requests or submit allegations to the opening agreement. The AEPD imposed a fine of EUR 2,000 for the Article 6(1) infringement.

The Dutch DPA received complaints that DPG Media Magazines (formerly Sanoma Media Netherlands) demanded a copy of an identity document before handling access or erasure requests made outside the secure login environment. DPG's policy always required the copy, did not offer the option of a redacted copy for digital requests, and left requests unhandled if no copy was supplied. The AP found this created unnecessary barriers and breached Article 12(2) GDPR. It imposed the base fine of EUR 525,000 under its category III fine policy, without increase or reduction. DPG stopped asking for ID copies on 17 December 2020 and uses a verification email instead.

A news report says the Austrian data protection authority imposed a fine of eight million euros on the REWE group over its 'jö Bonus Club' loyalty programme, citing GDPR violations. The decision is not final and REWE International AG says it will take legal action, denying responsibility for the data processing of the separate company jö. It is the second fine of this kind, after a EUR 2 million fine against the jö Bonus Club in summer 2021. The article does not describe the specific infringements or the reasoning.

The Garante received a report that the privacy notices published by the Frosinone local health authority named consent as the legal basis for processing patients' data for care purposes. Its investigation found further defects: missing or wrong legal bases, missing retention periods, a reference to legitimate interest and to data portability. The authority corrected the notices after the investigation began. The Garante declared the processing unlawful for breach of transparency and information duties (Arts 5(1)(a), 12, 13 GDPR), imposed no corrective measures because the conduct had ended, and fined the authority EUR 7,500 with publication of the decision.

A worker complained that the occupational health company appointed by his employer gave an irrelevant reply to his access request for his personal data and ignored a second request. The company only sent a copy of the health file in March 2021, after the Garante intervened. The Garante found breaches of the right of access and the deadline rules (Articles 12(3) and 15 GDPR) and fined the company EUR 4,000, ordering publication of the decision.

A press report revealed vulnerabilities in the Covid-19 screening platform and the 'Smart4You' app used by the Marche regional health authority: sequentially generated QR codes and a tax-code decoding function allowed third parties to see names, phone numbers and, in one case, a swab result. The authority notified a breach, and the Garante opened proceedings. It found breaches of integrity and confidentiality, security of processing and the duty to carry out a data protection impact assessment, plus Article 75 of the Italian Code. No corrective measures were ordered because the conduct had ended and remedies were adopted, but a fine of EUR 14,000 was imposed and the decision was ordered to be published.

A labour inspection by the Carabinieri found two working CCTV cameras inside the residential care home with no information signs. The controller, a cooperative, was charged with breaching the information duty under Article 13 GDPR. The company said the cameras were removed after the inspection. The Garante declared the processing unlawful and imposed a fine of EUR 1,000, taking into account the absence of prior violations and the company's cooperation. The Garante also ordered publication of the decision on its website.

A health manager employed by the local health authority complained that the authority published on its website a press release disclosing his personal data about disciplinary measures (suspension from service without pay) taken against him and another employee. The Garante held that the dissemination had no valid legal basis, since public bodies may disseminate personal data only where a law or regulation provides for it, and that the fact the data had already been in the press did not justify it. It found breaches of Articles 5 and 6 GDPR and Article 2-ter of the Code and fined the authority EUR 6,000. The decision is also ordered to be published on the Garante's website; no further corrective measures were needed as the publication had ended.

A complainant received a Type A military status certificate, issued on request for any lawful use, which stated that he had been exempted from military service. He argued that this disclosed sensitive data and was unnecessary for the certificate's purpose. The Authority held that a Type A certificate should only certify that the person has no remaining military obligations, so including the exemption breached the data minimisation principle in Article 5(1)(c) GDPR. It ordered the Ministry, as controller, to reissue the certificate stating only that the person has no military obligations. No fine was imposed.

The Finnish Data Protection Ombudsman's office opened the case on its own initiative after learning that Kymsote required prospective foster parents to obtain their police records through the right of access under the Criminal Data Protection Act and show the results to Kymsote. The deputy ombudsman found that this practice breached Article 6(1) and Article 10 GDPR, because Kymsote had no lawful basis for processing the data. The decision issues a reprimand and orders Kymsote to bring its processing into line within 30 days, which includes ending this procedure. No fine was imposed.

The UK DPA served the Ministry of Justice an Enforcement Notice to bring its processing into compliance by responding to data subjects' pending access requests and carrying out organisational changes to ensure that future ones are dealt with in the time frame provided for by Article 15 GDPR.

The European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS) issued a reprimand against the European Parliament for illegally transferring data to the US for having unclear cookies banners and therefore placing cookies without valid consent, having a data protection notice that did not comply with its transparency requirements, and failing to answer an access request by the complainants.

A driver asked the toll road operator Egnatia Odos in 2018 for photos and a logbook extract concerning an alleged unpaid toll. The company's first reply said the passage was recorded but refused to disclose it to a third party without a prosecutor's order and the Authority's permission. Only after the Authority intervened did the company provide a handwritten logbook entry and say no camera record existed. The Authority found the access request was answered late, outside the one-month period in Article 12(3) GDPR, and that the earlier reply was misleading. It imposed a fine of EUR 1,000.

A property owner complained that the Community Council had changed the mailing address for his flat without his consent, so that council bills were sent to his permanent residence elsewhere. The council's data protection officers first said there was a legal dispute and that the address was changed orally at his request. The investigation found that the change came from an electronic update from the Land Registry and that no legal dispute existed. The Commissioner found that the council breached Article 31 GDPR because its inconsistent statements, resulting from inadequate investigation, hindered the Commissioner's work, and imposed a fine of EUR 2,000.

A complaint was made about a judo coach posting on Facebook a video of a match involving a minor, without consent. The Commissioner asked the Pancyprian Judo Federation, to which the club belongs, for its policy and its position on the matter, sending a letter on 13 December 2021 and a reminder on 25 January 2022. The Federation did not respond, so a preliminary decision of 30 March 2022 found a failure to cooperate. The final decision found a breach of Article 31 GDPR and imposed a fine of EUR 5,000.
